prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT delay empiric antimicrobial therapy while awaiting imaging or LP results when bacterial meningitis is clinically suspected.

Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: a severe immunocompromised state (post-traumatic asplenia with incomplete pneumococcal immunisation) is an imaging-first criterion under WHO 2025 section A.4.
Do NOT rely on a negative Gram stain or a 'normal CT' to rule out bacterial meningitis when the clinical syndrome is present.
Do NOT treat with oral antibiotics alone; CNS penetration is inadequate for meningitis.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).

Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of age over 60 years, diabetes mellitus and the immunocompromised state (asplenia) (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.6.6); a negative Listeria PCR does not remove the indication for the empirical choice.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Continue for 4 days: Streptococcus pneumoniae is identified.
Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of a severe immunocompromised state (post-traumatic asplenia with incomplete pneumococcal immunisation) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, meningitis multiplex PCR, lactate) at the LP.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: stop ampicillin and continue ceftriaxone for 14 days for Streptococcus pneumoniae that is penicillin-resistant (MIC 0.12 ug/mL) and ceftriaxone-susceptible by CLSI meningitis breakpoints, which also explains the failure of oral amoxicillin (NICE NG240).
Place patient on droplet precautions until meningococcal disease is excluded.

Recognise asplenia: after recovery give pneumococcal conjugate vaccination (he has had a single PPSV23 dose 12 years ago), meningococcal ACWY and B and Hib vaccination, and provide written asplenia advice with standby antibiotics.
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or acute management of bacterial meningitis.
Echocardiography is not part of the meningitis work-up; nothing in the case suggests endocarditis.

PET imaging has no role in acute meningitis diagnosis; CT and MRI cover the indications.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker tool with no role in acute infectious meningitis.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, meningismus, and altered mental status; the full triad is present in only ~40%, so partial syndromes warrant aggressive workup.
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of a severe immunocompromised state (post-traumatic asplenia with incomplete pneumococcal immunisation) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).

A negative Gram stain does not exclude bacterial meningitis: sensitivity is about 85% with wide confidence limits (WHO 2025), lower after antibiotics; culture and multiplex PCR establish the organism.
A CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.4 or less is abnormally low (WHO 2025 A.2.2) and is more informative than the absolute value, above all in hyperglycemia.

Empirical therapy is ceftriaxone or cefotaxime within 60 minutes, with ampicillin when a Listeria risk factor (age over 60, pregnancy, immunocompromise) is present; vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance is locally prevalent (WHO 2025).

Asplenia (anatomic or functional) dramatically increases risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae); these patients require lifelong vaccination and a low threshold for empiric antibiotics.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Prior antibiotics reduce Gram-stain sensitivity and can sterilise the CSF; with neutrophilic pleocytosis, a low CSF:blood glucose ratio, raised CSF lactate and a positive pneumococcal PCR, the diagnosis remains bacterial meningitis.
red_herrings.data_point: Negative CSF Gram stain in a patient with prior oral antibiotic exposure
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest viral or aseptic meningitis and lower the threshold for withholding empiric antibiotics.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatremia is a common complication of bacterial meningitis itself (SIADH or cerebral salt wasting); assess volume status and correct it cautiously while the infection is treated. It does not point away from meningitis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Redirect workup toward primary endocrine or volume-status causes of hyponatremia.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Parameningeal sinus disease can be a SOURCE of pneumococcal meningitis, not an alternative diagnosis; the CSF profile remains the deciding evidence.
red_herrings.data_point: Bilateral maxillary sinus mucosal thickening on CT
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest uncomplicated sinusitis as the source of headache and fever, deferring meningitis evaluation.

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilledema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: a severe immunocompromised state (post-traumatic asplenia with incomplete pneumococcal immunisation); GCS is 13 with reactive pupils, no papilledema, no focal sign and no seizure, and age is not a criterion. NICE NG240 does not cover this patient (asplenia) and its 1.4.7 lists no trigger here; WHO 2025 governs this benchmark. Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose with dexamethasone come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.8).

clinical_pearls: In partially treated bacterial meningitis Gram stain sensitivity falls below its usual figure of about 85% (WHO 2025), making multiplex PCR critical for pathogen identification.
Asplenic patients should receive empiric coverage for encapsulated organisms until cultures definitively rule them out.
Dexamethasone benefit in bacterial meningitis is most strongly supported for pneumococcal disease and diminishes if given after antibiotics have been started.
A penicillin MIC of 0.12 ug/mL is resistant by CLSI meningitis breakpoints (no intermediate category), which explains failure of oral amoxicillin.

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Kenji Watanabe is a 68-year-old right-handed man with a history of splenectomy, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and gout who presents to the emergency department with progressive headache, confusion, and fever over approximately 24 hours. According to his wife, who accompanies him, the patient began complaining of a dull, bifrontal headache two days ago, which he attributed to a lingering upper respiratory infection he had been experiencing for about a week. He was seen by his primary care physician two days ago, who diagnosed likely sinusitis and started him on amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily. Over the past 24 hours, the headache has markedly intensified, becoming constant and rated 8 out of 10 in severity. His wife reports that he became progressively more confused throughout the day, initially repeating himself and seeming 'foggy,' then becoming difficult to arouse from sleep this evening. She also noted that he felt warm to touch, though his temperature at home was measured at only 37.9 degrees Celsius earlier in the day. He has complained of neck stiffness and has vomited twice in the past six hours. He has had no seizure activity, no weakness, no visual changes, and no rash. His wife specifically notes that his confusion is quite unlike him, as he is normally sharp and articulate. She decided to bring him to the emergency department when he was unable to recall their home address and appeared increasingly somnolent. Regarding his immunizations, he received only a single dose of Pneumovax 23 approximately 12 years ago without any subsequent boosters or conjugate vaccines.
